concepts.title: What is Factorisation
concepts.definition: When we factorise an algebraic expression, we write it as a product of factors. These factors may be numbers, algebraic variables or algebraic expressions. An irreducible factor is a factor which cannot be expressed further as a product of factors; in algebraic expressions we use the word irreducible in place of prime. Expressions like 3xy, 5x^2y, 2x(y + 2) are already in factor form.
concepts.formula: factorisation: expression = product of irreducible factors
concepts.key_idea: Factorising means writing an expression as a product of irreducible factors.

concepts.title: Method of Common Factors
concepts.definition: A systematic way of factorising an expression is the common factor method. It consists of three steps: (i) write each term of the expression as a product of irreducible factors; (ii) look for and separate the common factors; (iii) combine the remaining factors in each term in accordance with the distributive law. For example 2x + 4 = (2 x x) + (2 x 2) = 2(x + 2).
concepts.formula: common factor: a x m + a x n = a x (m + n)
concepts.key_idea: Pull out the factor common to every term using the distributive law.

concepts.title: Factorisation by Regrouping
concepts.definition: Sometimes all the terms in a given expression do not have a common factor, but the terms can be grouped in such a way that all the terms in each group have a common factor. When we do this, there emerges a common factor across all the groups leading to the required factorisation. For example 2xy + 2y + 3x + 3 = 2y(x + 1) + 3(x + 1) = (x + 1)(2y + 3). Rearranging the terms to allow grouping is called regrouping.

concepts.key_idea: Group pairs of terms so each group shares a factor, then pull out the shared bracket.

concepts.title: Factorisation Using Identities
concepts.definition: If an expression has a form that fits the right hand side of one of the identities, the left hand side gives the factorisation. Identity I: a^2 + 2ab + b^2 = (a + b)^2. Identity II: a^2 - 2ab + b^2 = (a - b)^2. Identity III: a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b). For example x^2 + 8x + 16 = (x + 4)^2, 4y^2 - 12y + 9 = (2y - 3)^2, 49p^2 - 36 = (7p - 6)(7p + 6).
concepts.key_idea: Recognise perfect squares and difference of squares to factor instantly.

concepts.title: Factors of the Form (x + a)(x + b)
concepts.definition: Expressions like x^2 + 5x + 6 are of the form x^2 + (a + b)x + ab. Identity IV: (x + a)(x + b) = x^2 + (a + b)x + ab. For factorising x^2 + px + q, we find two factors a and b of the constant term q such that ab = q and a + b = p; then the factors are (x + a) and (x + b).
concepts.formula: (x + a)(x + b) = x^2 + (a + b)x + ab; find ab = q and a + b = p

concepts.title: Division of a Monomial by a Monomial
concepts.definition: Division is the inverse operation of multiplication. To divide a monomial by a monomial, write both in irreducible factor form and cancel the common factors: 6x^3 divided by 2x = (2 x 3 x x x x x)/(2 x x) = 3x^2. Since 2x x 3x^2 = 6x^3, therefore 6x^3 divided by 2x = 3x^2.
concepts.key_idea: Cancel common factors; coefficients divide, powers subtract.

concepts.title: Division of a Polynomial by a Monomial
concepts.definition: In the case of division of a polynomial by a monomial, we may carry out the division either by dividing each term of the polynomial by the monomial or by the common factor method. For example (4y^3 + 5y^2 + 6y) divided by 2y = 4y^3/2y + 5y^2/2y + 6y/2y = 2y^2 + (5/2)y + 3.

concepts.title: Division of a Polynomial by a Polynomial
concepts.definition: In the case of division of a polynomial by a polynomial, we cannot proceed by dividing each term of the dividend by the divisor. Instead, we factorise both the polynomials and cancel their common factors. For example (7x^2 + 14x) divided by (x + 2): factorise 7x^2 + 14x = 7x(x + 2), then cancel to get 7x. We consider only divisions in which the remainder is zero, where Dividend = Divisor x Quotient.
